slides.heading: Six letters that tell you where a word came from
body: Six consonants, and every one doubles a sound you have.
They mark a word as old, formal, or borrowed.
A vowel with a built-in ending, and a sign that silences a letter.

slides.heading: Pen and paper
body: Real paper, a real pen.
Both halves of the name, out loud.
Six shapes, and the sounds are already yours.

slides.heading: Why Thai kept six letters it could have dropped
body: English keeps the p in *psychology* for exactly this reason.
Thai took religious and scholarly words from Sanskrit and Pali.
The words kept their spelling, and the script made room.
Each of the six tells you about the word rather than the sound.

slides.heading: Two of them live up at the temple
body: Two at the temple, four at the harbour.
The temple pair both write **s**.
Thai has three s letters at the temple, and you already have one.

slides.heading: The pavilion with a pennant
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means a **pavilion**.
The tiger's s, from a second temple letter.
The buffalo's letter with **a flag stroke planted on top**.

slides.heading: The hermit carrying his basket
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means a **hermit**.
The third and last temple s.
The leaf's letter, **crossed with one line**.

slides.heading: Write both, and put the third one beside them
body: The pavilion: **the buffalo, with a stroke planted on top**.
The hermit: **the leaf's letter, crossed once**.
Put the tiger under them both, and look at the column.

slides.heading: The temple's other half, and it is one tone for both lengths
body: Temple letter, dead syllable, **low tone**.
Long vowel or short, the tone comes out the same.
The harbour needed two rules here. The temple needs one.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: Tray plus short ee, then mast, pavilion, hermit.
Two syllables, and a different rule for each.
**Out loud before you turn it over.**

slides.heading: That one
body: **พิเศษ** — special.
First half: harbour, dead, short — high.
Second half: temple, dead, long — low.
The hermit's letter closes the word instead of opening it.

slides.heading: And four of them live down at the water
body: Four at the harbour, low class, and no new tone rules.
A second n, a second y, a second breathed p, a second breathed t.
Shape and sound each, and both are already familiar.

slides.heading: The novice on the pier
body: The word means a **novice monk**.
The mouse's n, and the two sound identical.
It closes a syllable with a hum, so the syllable stays live.
A whole **chicken frame first**, and the mouse's loop last.

slides.heading: The woman on the harbour wall
body: The word means a **woman**.
The giant's y at the front of a syllable.
The novice's loop is attached; this one hangs **a free curl underneath**.
Put it last in a syllable and it lands as **n**.

slides.heading: The junk with its anchor out
body: The word means a **Chinese junk ship**.
The tray's breathed ph, from the harbour.
The bag coils its head inside the frame. This one **hangs it outside**.

slides.heading: The flag knotted shut
body: The word means a **flag**.
The soldier's breathed th, from the harbour.
The boat's letter with **its top tied into a crossed loop**.

slides.heading: Write all four
body: The novice: **chicken frame, then the mouse's loop**.
The woman: **the same frame, with a free curl underneath**.
The junk: **the bag, with its head swung outside**.
The flag: **the boat, with its top tied shut**.
slides.thai: ณ ญ ภ ธ

slides.heading: Read this one
body: Junk, long post, hermit, long post.
One harbour letter and one temple letter, in one word.
Both halves run live. **Out loud before you turn it over.**

slides.heading: That one
body: **ภาษา** — a language.
First half: harbour, live — flat.
Second half: temple, live — rising.

slides.heading: ำ, the vowel with an ending packed inside it
body: A small ring on the roof, and the long post behind it.
It says a short ah, and then an **m**.
The m is built in. Nothing is written for it.

slides.heading: Which means every syllable it finishes is live
body: The syllable ends on a hum, so the air keeps running.
Every syllable this vowel finishes is **live**.
Short as it is, the hum keeps the air running, so the syllable lives.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: Tiger plus the new vowel, then buffalo, the curl on the roof, and the woman's letter.
**Remember what she does last in a syllable.**
Both tones before you speak.

slides.heading: That one
body: **สำคัญ** — important.
First half: temple, live — rising.
Second half: harbour, live — flat.
The woman's letter lands as **n**, and the hum keeps it live.

slides.heading: เ-อ, which stands on both sides at once
body: The mast on the front steps, the basin in the back yard.
One vowel standing on **both sides** of its consonant.
An **er with no r in it**, throat loose, held long.

slides.heading: And what happens when something follows it
body: The basin steps aside, and a **brim appears on the roof**.
The mast in front stays exactly where it was.
Same vowel, same length, one room different.

slides.heading: Except when the final is the giant's letter
body: Before the giant's letter, the basin drops and **nothing replaces it**.
Mast, consonant, giant — and the vowel is unwritten.
**เลย** is the 81st commonest word in Thai and spelled exactly that way.

slides.heading: The short one, and an honest gap
body: **เ-อะ** — mast, consonant, basin, then the two hooks.
Common Thai has no closed example of it.
Learn the open shape and move on.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: Mast, the child's letter, the brim above, the mouse closing it.
**Name the vowel first**, then the district, then the tone.

slides.heading: That one
body: **เดิน** — to walk.
The long vowel in its closed shape, brim on the roof.
Market letter, live syllable, flat.

slides.heading: The sign that switches a letter off
body: A small sign above a letter, and the letter goes silent.
The spelling survives on the page, and the mouth ignores it.
**สัตว์** — animal. Three consonants written, two spoken.
**ศูนย์** — zero, with the giant's letter locked shut.

slides.heading: One word for each of the six
body: **อากาศ** — air, or the weather. The pavilion's letter closing it as a t-stop.
**ศูนย์** — zero. The pavilion opening a word instead, with the giant locked shut behind.
**พิเศษ** — special. The hermit's letter stopping the word dead.
**คุณ** — you, politely. The novice's letter closing it with a hum.
**ญาติ** — a relative. The woman's letter opening it, and the vowel written last is never said.
**ภาพ** — a picture. The junk opening it, and the tray stopping it dead.
**วิธี** — a method, or a way of doing something. The flag's letter opens the second half.

slides.prompt: ศึกษา is read sùek-sǎa — low, then rising. Both halves open with a temple s letter. So what makes the two tones come out different?

answers: First half: stopped by the chicken, so dead — low.
Second half: open long vowel, so live — rising.
Both temple rules in a single word.

slides.prompt: สัตว์ is read sàt, one closed syllable. Its spelling ends on the buffalo's letter under a small sign. What is that sign doing, and what would be lost without it?

answers: It silences the letter beneath it.
Left unmarked, the letter would be read, and the word would be wrong.
Dropped, the word would lose the spelling it arrived with.
The mark keeps the history on the page and out of the mouth.

slides.heading: Thirty-four letters, and the temple finished
body: **ศ** pavilion, **ษ** hermit, **ณ** novice, **ญ** woman, **ภ** junk, **ธ** flag.
Thirty-four consonants, and every tone class now complete.
**ำ** carries its own m, **เ-อ** wraps around, and **์** silences.
Next: the last ten letters, and two the language has retired.
